ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Institutional Review board of Boston University Medical Center.

Loneliness is common; approximately one-third of the adult US population >45 years old and approximately 43% of adults >60 years old report loneliness. 1, 3 Loneliness is associated with a range of negative health outcomes, including dementia, 4, 5 sleep disturbances, 6 coronary heart disease, 7 stroke, [8] [9] [10] and cardiovascular disease. 11 Further, loneliness has been linked to detrimental behavioral changes, such as physical inactivity 12, 13 and smoking, 13, 14 and with depression. 15 Loneliness may influence biological pathways that lead to atherosclerosis, 16, 17 hypertension, 16, 18 and metabolic disease. [19] [20] [21] Few population-based studies have evaluated the prospective relationship between loneliness and incident stroke. 8, 9 Using data from the UK Biobank, 9 investigators observed that over a 7-year follow up period lonely participants had a higher risk of incident stroke after controlling for age, sex, diastolic and systolic blood pressure, smoking, physical inactivity, and alcohol consumption.

Cohort (Gen 3 Cohort), including grandchildren of the Original Cohort, were recruited in 2002 along with the NOS cohort (spouses of members of the Offspring Cohort who were not in the original Offspring Cohort).

FHS participants were examined on average every 2-8 years (Original every 2 years; Offspring and Omni 1 every 4-8 years; Gen 3, NOS, and Omni 2 every 6 years), including medical history, physical examination, anthropometry, assessment of psychosocial factors by questionnaire, and 12-lead electrocardiography.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=0.07", "p=0.6", "p=0.17"), Sentence = c("We observed significant interactions between age (<80 versus ≥80) and each of prior and baseline loneliness (p = 0.02 and p=0.07, respectively) in their associations with incident stroke.", "There was no interaction between sex and either prior loneliness (p=0.6) or baseline loneliness (p=0.17).", "There was no interaction between sex and either prior loneliness (p=0.6) or baseline loneliness (p=0.17)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::
